items.rss_title: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline
items.rss_description: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline Talent Gap ITL Editorial Team Tue, 11/17/2026 - 11:05 As AI automates entry-level insurance tasks, insurance industry leaders must design experiences to develop professional judgment in emerging talent. November 19, 2026 Image Back in the '90s, I was a beast at reconciling spreadsheets. The 10 fingers I'm using to type these lines used to set my "10-key" numeric keypad ablaze. But if you're among the younger readers to come across this article, you'll have no idea what I'm talking about. And as a society, I think that's for the best. A core promise of technological advancement is to eliminate drudgery, like using a 10-key to enter vast amounts of numeric data. In property and casualty insurance, we have spent decades trying to remove mundane work from the lives of underwriters, claims professionals, and technologists. We made great strides with Robotic Process Automation (RPA), leaps with broader Intelligent Automation (IA), and now a phenomenal bound with Artificial Intelligence (AI), which promises to revolutionize the way we work. But amid the terrific change lurks an industry-scale problem. While our job definitions and related skills are morphing at an absurdly fast rate, how do we ensure that emerging talent has the opportunity to develop the depth of understanding and judgment their predecessors possess, even while AI is tending to disassociate humans from some of the traditional activities of their craft? That replacement system needs a name and, more importantly, an owner. Architecting Experience is the framework of deliberately designed exposures, decisions, and feedback loops through which people develop professional judgment and decision context. Cracks in the career ladder Stanford's Digital Economy Lab analyzed payroll data on millions of U.S. jobs through June 2026 and found no economy-wide displacement from AI. What they did find was new employment among 22- to 25-year-olds lagging in industries heavily affected by AI, by about 19% compared to less-affected industries.[1] The employment ladder isn't broken, but some rungs at the bottom are disappearing, which makes it a whole lot harder to climb. Even where junior positions aren't disappearing, the formative skills they help develop are the easiest to automate. In insurance, applied experience and apprenticeship have built the tacit knowledge and judgment needed for success for generations. After ingesting enough submissions, you develop a second sense for when a detail looks off, or when risks that look identical stem from entirely different causes. But when this repetitive and seemingly menial work is delegated to AI, younger staff are deprived of the very task-level experiences they need to develop the business EQ, empathy, and scar tissue that will someday make them senior. What our young talent are left with are the tasks too difficult for AI, and sometimes beyond the judgment they possess. In their 2026 AI Jobs Barometer, PwC looked at over a billion job advertisements. They found that heavily AI-exposed entry-level roles were seven times more likely to demand senior capabilities—like judgment, leadership, and interpersonal skills—than the jobs least exposed to AI. PwC described the trend as the "seniorization" of junior work.[2] A short-term view of AI-driven task optimization will only make the problem worse. For senior employees, more demanding tasks feel more meaningful and engaging than rote work. But the type of work that is most interesting to a seasoned professional isn't necessarily the type of work best suited to creating one. And meaningful work sounds wonderful until every task is a demanding one, and the much-needed Easy Tuesday becomes as much of a relic as my most trusty 10-digit keypad. Clear the slop from the stream BCG recently surveyed 11,749 workers across 14 markets about their use of AI at work. Two-thirds of regular AI users reported increased job satisfaction. At the same time, 41% reported increased mental strain. Half said they were spending more time managing and directing AI than doing the underlying work itself.[3] "Brain fry" refers to the mental fatigue associated with information overload from increased AI oversight.[4] With AI, any junior underwriter can generate a 40-page report with the aplomb of a managing director. But then, the report has to be checked. Preferably by someone with enough know-how to identify and correct mistakes. Without guardrails, we quickly end up in a system where our young talent can access AI-powered tools that allow them to produce work that looks good, but is actually riddled with problems. These problems are then sent upstream to more senior resources who have to spend their time fixing this "workslop"[5]. Junior professionals learn nothing in the process, and increase the workload of their most knowledgeable, and often most expensive, colleagues. When we claim AI is changing the way we work, we're giving the tool too much credit, while absolving ourselves of responsibility. The truth is, AI isn't changing the way we work. Our decision-makers are. And if, as a result of these changes and the adoption of AI, the leaders break the career ladder, they are responsible for engineering a new one. AI-resilient architecture I'm not in favor of clinging to rote work out of nostalgia. AI very much has a place in our workflows, and I remain bullish on the beneficial role of AI over the long term. But today, as we are all still sorting out the impacts and influences of AI on real people, we must think things through holistically and humanistically from the very beginning. In the face of AI removing traditional and lower-level tasks, the implications of this must be assessed, and solutions for the resultant gaps must be created. When architecting experience for new talent, what matters is to look at tasks through the dual lens of raw efficiency and professional development. Do the tasks teach the rules of the game, and more importantly, when the rules stop applying? Do they offer a chance to shadow a more seasoned professional to develop situational awareness and understanding of context? Do they help build judgment? Do they create the kinds of relationships every business is built on? These answers will help inform which tasks to automate, and which need more thought. A "yes" doesn't mean the task cannot be handed off to automation; it means the developmental value has to be preserved, somehow. The oversight role for management is to understand and enforce the right order of operations: organic brain first, neural network second. As with all complex systems, architecting experience isn't a blueprint. It's a process bound to yield different results for different organizations. Once the initial assessment is complete, ideally under the supervision of an executive with accountability, the hard work of execution, review, and adaptation begins. The good news is: there's plenty of responsibility to go around. Executive management must identify the experiences that create expertise, design a plan for succession, and own how the business will look ten years down the road. Elsewhere, HR and development teams have a responsibility to engineer the learning experiences and coaching or apprenticeship infrastructure, while managers can iterate, suggest improvements, and raise the red flag when skills aren't being developed. Tech and risk teams also have a clear role to observe AI usage, monitor costs and defect rates, and flag when automated work misses the mark. Senior professionals must keep in mind that juniors need engagement, context, and good professional models to follow, while the juniors themselves must remember to think first and ask AI second. Insurance is still early in the AI adoption process, and fortunate to have a deep bench of experienced professionals around the world, alongside ambitious newcomers. But every day, AI offers new deployment opportunities for efficiency and optimization. The greatest organizations of tomorrow will not only be able to harness those opportunities, but will also succeed in architecting experience for the next generation of world-class talent. References 1. Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, and Ruyu Chen. Stanford Digital Economy Lab. "Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence." Revised Aug. 12, 2026. Source 2. PwC. "2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer." June 15, 2026. Source 3. Boston Consulting Group. "AI at Work: Strategy Matters More Than Tools." June 3, 2026. Source 4. Boston Consulting Group and UC Riverside research, reported in Harvard Business Review. "When Using AI Leads to 'Brain Fry.'" March 2026. Source 5. BetterUp Labs and Stanford Social Media Lab. "Workslop: The Hidden Cost of AI-Generated Busywork." Sept. 15, 2025. Source Bob Pick

items.title: What If 'Doomsday' Isn't Just the Next Marvel Hit?
items.original_title: What If 'Doomsday' Isn't Just the Next Marvel Hit?
items.rss_title: What If 'Doomsday' Isn't Just the Next Marvel Hit?
items.rss_description: What If 'Doomsday' Isn't Just the Next Marvel Hit? Risk Management ITL Editorial Team Tue, 11/17/2026 - 15:02 Households once ran on a checkbook, a stamp, and a Saturday trip to the bank. Could your company run that way again if it had to? November 19, 2026 Image On Dec. 18, Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters, and millions of us will happily pay to watch Earth's mightiest heroes face a villain bent on bringing the world to its knees. It's a great escape, partly because we know the heroes always show up in time. Real life offers no such guarantee, and last week showed how close we already live to our own doomsday script. Consider how recently the world ran on paper. Not long ago, people received a printed paycheck every week. Many of us remember our parents planning lunch hours around getting to the bank, or racing there Saturday morning before the branch closed at noon. Bills were paid by paper check, mailed to the mortgage company, the electric company and the oil company. Insuring a car or a house meant calling an agent. Buying anything "from a computer" was pure Isaac Asimov. Today, the entirety of human knowledge fits in a device the size of a deck of cards that nearly everyone carries in their pocket. That has been liberating. But it has also left us almost completely dependent on invisible systems we assume will always be on and safe from disruption, whether the threat is a malfunction, a cyberattack or simple human error. The past week showed how quickly those systems can grind to a halt. On Nov. 12, a Microsoft outage took down Outlook, Teams and Copilot – the backbone of millions of businesses – across dozens of countries for more than half a day. The next afternoon, a communications failure forced the FAA to ground every departing U.S. flight for more than four hours, the longest nationwide shutdown since 9/11. Then on Nov. 16, a software bug in JPMorgan Chase's own hardware disrupted online banking, branch transactions and Zelle payments, spilling over to customers at other banks doing business with Chase. Chase said there was no evidence the outage was cyber-related, and that is exactly the point. If an internal glitch can rattle America's biggest commercial bank, imagine what a deliberate, coordinated attack on power grids, water systems and communications networks could do. Governments urge households to keep emergency supplies, including cash, on hand. Is your company following the same advice? Do business continuity plans cover this? For many companies, the honest answer is "not really." Most plans are built for hurricanes, fires, the loss of a building and other localized events. Backups reside in another state, employees work from home, and operations shift to a recovery site. All of this assumes the Internet, the power grid, and the rest of the economy are still working somewhere . Financial regulators have pushed for more. In 2019, the FFIEC reframed its guidance from business continuity planning to business continuity management, with a focus on operational resilience and the ripple effects of outages across the financial system. The industry also created Sheltered Harbor , a standard for backing up critical customer account data nightly to an offline, air-gapped vault so customers can still reach their funds after a worst-case cyber event. Sheltered Harbor is now winding down, with its specification moving to its parent, FS-ISAC, but the principle stands. Still, even these measures assume someone, somewhere, can restore the data and run the systems. A nationwide, prolonged outage is a scenario few plans address head-on. Can companies function when the rest of the world can't? Not entirely. If customers can't reach essential services, payment rails are down and vendors go dark, no amount of preparation will preserve business as usual. But "not entirely" is materially different from "not at all." The goal is keeping your promises: knowing who your customers are, what they own and what you owe them, and honoring the most critical obligations through manual processes until systems return. That is what makes recovery possible, and it preserves trust when it matters most. Building on the plan you already have Organizations don't need to start over. items.title: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps
items.original_title: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps
items.rss_title: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps
items.rss_description: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps Cyber ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/18/2026 - 14:34 The $6.3 billion Binance theft bypassed private keys entirely, exposing gaps in how crypto risks are underwritten and covered. November 19, 2026 Image On Oct. 29, attackers took roughly $6.3 billion out of Binance's hot wallets in about 20 minutes. It is the largest crypto theft on record, and the FBI has tied it to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. Binance has since committed to absorbing the financial impact of the incident. By Oct. 31, it reported that 98% of the affected token assets had been replenished. How it happened matters more than how much According to Binance's incident report, the campaign ran for months. One engineer installed a tampered developer tool in June. Another was compromised in September through a fake coding assignment. In October, the attackers used an internal AI tool to get into more machines and finally took control of the system that approves wallet transactions. The key detail for insurance: Binance says no private keys were stolen. The attackers didn't need them. They controlled the system that signs transactions, so it signed whatever the attackers asked. Underwriting conversations with crypto clients have long centered on keys. Where are they stored? Who holds them? How many people have to sign off? This loss shows that everything around the keys (people, laptops, software and approval systems) matters just as much. What this means for the insurance market Tougher questions. Crime and specie applications will dig into employee devices, developer tools, and internal AI tools. Underwriters will want to know who can push code into live systems and how fast a wallet can be frozen once something looks wrong. More caution on hot wallets. Offline cold storage has always been easier to insure than online hot wallets used for everyday withdrawals. After watching billions leave hot wallets in minutes, insurers will be more careful about how much limit they put there and what they charge. More disputes over which policy pays. Crypto losses tend to fall between cyber and crime policies, and this attack sits right on the line. Cyber or crime? Four common mix-ups "We have cyber, so a hack is covered." Cyber pays for the cleanup - forensics, legal advice, customer notices, data lawsuits, and lost income while systems are down. Most cyber policies exclude the theft or transfer of funds, and many exclude digital assets. Cyber may pay for the investigation but not the stolen assets. "We have crime, so theft is covered." A standard crime policy protects money, securities and other property. Without an endorsement, crypto may not clearly fit. Specie policies often cover cold storage only, with hot wallets excluded or sublimited. "Computer fraud and funds transfer fraud are the same thing." They aren't. Computer fraud usually needs a hacker to change data or force a transfer. Funds transfer fraud usually involves fake instructions sent to a bank. An exchange signing its own blockchain transaction may not fit neatly into either. "Our people were tricked, so social engineering coverage applies." Expect a debate. Social engineering coverage usually responds when an employee is fooled into sending money, often with a small sublimit. Here, engineers were tricked into installing bad software, not sending funds. What brokers should review before the next renewal Map the gaps. Lay the crime, specie, cyber, tech E&O, and D&O policies side by side and walk through this scenario. Who pays for the stolen assets, the forensics, and the lawsuits? Check the "other insurance" clauses, since cyber and crime policies sometimes each point to the other. Compare limits to real exposure. Ask how much the client keeps in hot wallets on a normal day and a busy day, then compare that to the limit they're buying. Talk about the reserve fund. Many exchanges keep their own fund to repay customers. That isn't insurance, and if it's held in crypto, its value can drop right when it's needed. Don't forget D&O. Lawsuits and regulators usually follow a large loss, often in more than one country. Directors and officers will want to know their coverage holds up. Looking ahead There is some good news here. About $2.85 billion of the stolen funds has been frozen or intercepted, mostly stablecoins whose issuers can block them, and Binance has said customers will be covered. Insurance capacity for digital asset companies keeps growing. More insurers are willing to write crime, specie and D&O for crypto businesses than a few years ago, and one event shouldn't reverse that. But more capacity doesn't mean easier terms. This single loss accounts for nearly three-quarters of the crypto hacking losses recorded this year. Headline events like this make underwriters more careful. Expect longer applications, more underwriting meetings and a closer look at how controls work day to day. Vague answers will cost you. For brokers, the job is easy to describe and hard to do. Understand how the client actually operates, not just where the keys are kept, and make sure the coverage matches. The clients who can show their work will get the best of the new capacity. The next renewal is the right time to start that conversation. Ben Slagis

items.summary: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps Cyber ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/18/2026 - 14:34 The $6.3 billion Binance theft bypassed private keys entirely, exposing gaps in how crypto risks are underwritten and covered. November 19, 2026 Image On Oct. 29, attackers took roughly $6.3 billion out of Binance's hot wallets in about 20 minutes. It is the largest crypto theft on record, and the FBI has tied it to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. Binance has since committed to absorbing the financial impact of the incident. By Oct. 31, it reported that 98% of the affected token assets had been replenished. How it happened matters more than how much According to Binance's incident report, the campaign ran for months. One engineer installed a tampered developer tool in June. Another was compromised in September through a fake coding assignment. In October, the attackers used an internal AI tool to get into more machines and finally took control of the system that approves wallet transactions. The key detail for insurance: Binance says no private keys were stolen. The attackers didn't need them. They controlled the system that signs transactions, so it signed whatever the attackers asked. Underwriting conversations with crypto clients have long centered on keys. Where are they stored? Who holds them? How many people have to sign off? This loss shows that everything around the keys (people, laptops, software and approval systems) matters just as much. What this means for the insurance market Tougher questions. Crime and specie applications will dig into employee devices, developer tools, and internal AI tools. Underwriters will want to know who can push code into live systems and how fast a wallet can be frozen once something looks wrong. More caution on hot wallets. Offline cold storage has always been easier to insure than online hot wallets used for everyday withdrawals. After watching billions leave hot wallets in minutes, insurers will be more careful about how much limit they put there and what they charge. More disputes over which policy pays. Crypto losses tend to fall between cyber and crime policies, and this attack sits right on the line. Cyber or crime? Four common mix-ups "We have cyber, so a hack is covered." Cyber pays for the cleanup - forensics, legal advice, customer notices, data lawsuits, and lost income while systems are down. Most cyber policies exclude the theft or transfer of funds, and many exclude digital assets. Cyber may pay for the investigation but not the stolen assets. "We have crime, so theft is covered." A standard crime policy protects money, securities and other property. Without an endorsement, crypto may not clearly fit. Specie policies often cover cold storage only, with hot wallets excluded or sublimited. "Computer fraud and funds transfer fraud are the same thing." They aren't. Computer fraud usually needs a hacker to change data or force a transfer. Funds transfer fraud usually involves fake instructions sent to a bank. An exchange signing its own blockchain transaction may not fit neatly into either. "Our people were tricked, so social engineering coverage applies." Expect a debate. Social engineering coverage usually responds when an employee is fooled into sending money, often with a small sublimit. Here, engineers were tricked into installing bad software, not sending funds. What brokers should review before the next renewal Map the gaps. Lay the crime, specie, cyber, tech E&O, and D&O policies side by side and walk through this scenario. Who pays for the stolen assets, the forensics, and the lawsuits? Check the "other insurance" clauses, since cyber and crime policies sometimes each point to the other. Compare limits to real exposure. Ask how much the client keeps in hot wallets on a normal day and a busy day, then compare that to the limit they're buying. Talk about the reserve fund. Many exchanges keep their own fund to repay customers. That isn't insurance, and if it's held in crypto, its value can drop right when it's needed. Don't forget D&O. Lawsuits and regulators usually follow a large loss, often in more than one country. Directors and officers will want to know their coverage holds up. Looking ahead There is some good news here. About $2.85 billion of the stolen funds has been frozen or intercepted, mostly stablecoins whose issuers can block them, and Binance has said customers will be covered. Insurance capacity for digital asset companies keeps growing. More insurers are willing to write crime, specie and D&O for crypto businesses than a few years ago, and one event shouldn't reverse that. But more capacity doesn't mean easier terms. This single loss accounts for nearly three-quarters of the crypto hacking losses recorded this year. Headline events like this make underwriters more careful. Expect longer applications, more underwriting meetings and a closer look at how controls work day to day. Vague answers will cost you. For brokers, the job is easy to describe and hard to do. Understand how the client actually operates, not just where the keys are kept, and make sure the coverage matches. The clients who can show their work will get the best of the new capacity. The next renewal is the right time to start that conversation. Ben Slagis

items.title: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start
items.original_title: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start
items.rss_title: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start
items.rss_description: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start Agent & Broker ITL Editorial Team Tue, 11/17/2026 - 15:15 Four-year producer retention has sat near 14% for years. One overlooked cause: new producers are handed materials that promote the company but give prospects no reason to trust the person. November 19, 2026 Image Even with aptitude and personality testing, only about 14% of new financial professionals have still been under contract four years after they were hired, according to LIMRA. The losses come early. First-year retention runs from 44% to 55%, depending on who recruited the producer. When a new producer leaves within two years, the recruiting effort, the licensing, the training, and the manager's time are lost. The industry has refined selection, adjusted financing plans, and built mentoring programs. Yet the four-year number has barely moved. I spent more than 25 years in this industry as a producer, a wholesaler, and a group long-term care presenter. I've come to believe we're overlooking one piece of the problem: the gap between marketing and sales. Marketing departments produce great materials that promote the brand and its products. But those materials don't help producers distinguish themselves from colleagues who hand out the same materials. The most successful practices are built on trust. A prospect won't discuss their financial or insurance problems until they trust the producer enough to reveal highly personal information. Insurance companies have a reputation for being conservative and not on the leading edge of new technology. Perhaps it's in our DNA as managers of risk. There has always been a tension between what we can do and what we're allowed to do: a tug of war between sales and compliance. What leaders say keeps producers In a 2022 study, LIMRA and Finseca asked field and home-office leaders which factors do the most to keep new producers past year two. They named five: early activity (a fast start), a strong selection process before hiring, joint field work, quality sales skills training, and mentoring. Field leaders also listed lack of early activity among the causes of termination. Four of those five factors are about the producer: who we hire and how we train and support them. Early activity is different. It depends on two people: the producer must reach out, and the prospect has to respond. Prospects respond to people they feel a connection with. What constitutes activity? When I began, it meant 10 meetings a week with new prospects, all of them in person. You left behind a business card and a generic company brochure and hoped you'd made enough of an impression to earn a second appointment. Today, a new producer may reach out in person or virtually. Either way, the takeaway must be memorable. A business card or marketing piece that provides an experience rather than just data can raise a producer's MQ (memorability quotient) significantly. The format gap Producers are largely on their own in building trust, and the materials they're handed don't help much. The World Life Insurance Report 2027, published in September 2026 by Capgemini and LIMRA, surveyed 6,175 consumers in 18 countries. More than 40% of those considering coverage felt confused, uncertain, or unconvinced by what they found, and one in four dropped out before buying. Overly technical language was the top reason, cited by 37%. Eighty-five percent of those consumers want to interact with an advisor at some point, and two-thirds prefer a human advisor when they finalize coverage. The demand for the producer is there. The materials can get in the way instead of advancing the relationship. Research shows what helps. In an experiment by the Society of Actuaries Research Institute and RGA, summaries, FAQs, and simple icons raised comprehension by 21%. Interactive elements, such as a needs calculator, raised it by 28%. On a page that used both, adding video raised it another 15%. Imagine delivering all that through something as simple as a business card. People, both prospects and producers, differ in many ways. Finding commonality is key to establishing a relationship. Half of consumers in the Capgemini–LIMRA study said they prefer advisors with similar demographic characteristics. And in the SOA–RGA experiment, comprehension rose significantly when participants saw the presenter as credible, expert, and from a similar cultural background. As a long-term care insurance wholesaler, I often funded advisors' client events: dinners meant to turn prospects into clients. Most guests didn't know the advisor or had only a passing acquaintance with him. At one event I sponsored, the advisor spent little time presenting himself and concentrated on the features and benefits of the coverage from the company I represented. He didn't convert a single prospect, and I got zero return on my investment. The guests had no reason to trust the person in front of them, so the product never had a chance. We can't know in advance who is on the other end of a producer's outreach. Some prospects read. Some watch. Some listen. Some need to try a calculator before they believe anything. The safest approach is to offer something for each of them, with the producer's own face and voice up front. Conventional e-newsletters contribute to inbox glut Most new producers are sent out with the same tools as everyone else: a business card, perhaps a company newsletter, and a set of pre-approved PDFs. The newsletter is the piece most firms count on to keep prospects warm, and it has five weaknesses. They are too long. Attention spans are short, and screen after screen asks for more time than most readers will give. They make readers scroll to choose. Readers scroll down to see what's there, then back up to decide. Many give up first. They are mostly text. Email can carry video and interactive tools, but few firms use them. Prospects who would rather watch or listen find little to engage them. They lack creative calls to action or lead magnets of value. Readers see a "Subscribe" or "Get my 5 tips" button as permission to receive spam. They speak for the company, not the person. Prospects learn about the carrier's strength and products, but nothing about the producer who sent it. There is also a compliance cost. Approved PDFs get downloaded, forwarded, and kept long after they've been revised. A PDF attached in March can still be circulating in October, carrying last spring's disclosure. Meanwhile, new producers who need to be noticed improvise with homemade posts and flyers. Producers need to be seen, and compliance needs control. A better newsletter respects the reader's time: one page with links to no more than three pieces of content. At a glance, the reader sees each title, whether it's an article, a video, or a podcast, and about how long it will take. They choose in seconds, without scrolling, in the format they prefer. And because the pieces are links, not downloads, compliance retains more control. What a first impression could be Social media posts, newsletters, mail, and product information all have their place in the sales cycle, but on their own, none of them builds a relationship. Today's technology can ease the tension between sales and compliance. Personal profiles with video and text, built on a company-approved template, let every producer present themselves authentically by email, on social media and websites, and through "phygital" marketing: digital content delivered through physical objects such as business cards, printed materials, or promotional merchandise. An agency or firm can start with business cards, where a scan or a tap opens a short personal video scripted to feature the "who" and not the "what" along with their bio, contact information, and compliance-approved content. Data alone isn't memorable. Experiences are. The company brochure can travel the same way. Printed brochures are costly and usually end up in the circular file. The same approved piece can live behind the producer's card instead, with no reprint charges, unlimited distribution, and home-office updates that take effect everywhere at once. Stories engage far better than statistics. Say a new producer targets young couples buying their first home who need to protect their mortgage. They need life insurance, and so do growing families and pre-retirees who want to transfer wealth efficiently. A firm could offer a choice of short, approved videos, each speaking to a different audience, that drop into the same approved brochure that explains different types of life insurance. Then add a lead gate, a short form that asks for a prospect's contact details in exchange for content of value. In large organizations, lead gates usually sit on the company website, not on individual producers' pages, so the contact information goes to the company or agency. Placed in the producer's own piece, a lead gate helps a new producer build a prospect list from the first week. Put together, these elements give a new producer something memorable that builds trust: a personal profile, an approved multimedia brochure, and a way to find the people worth calling. No study yet measures the effect directly, but the evidence points the same way. What leaders can do now None of this requires a new distribution model. It requires looking at a new producer's first 90 days from the prospect's side of the table. Audit the first impression. Gather everything a new producer can send a prospect in week one. Then ask: Why would I choose this producer over another? Put the person up front. Give each new producer a short video or audio introduction about who they are, not what they do. All your producers do similar work. Who they are is what sets them apart. Cover every format. Pair each key message with something to read, something to watch or hear, and something to try. In a newsletter, that means no more than three pieces, each labeled with its format and length. Host it; don't attach it. Sharing content by link keeps the company in control and ensures only approved, up-to-date materials circulate. Watch the early signals. Lack of activity is an early warning sign, and analytics can now measure it. Managers can see which channels drive activity and which new recruits may need help sooner. Have it ready before the first appointment. A fast start depends on what the producer can share in the first week, not the first quarter. Give them something worth answering Pushing prospects with a stick instead of offering a carrot gives the industry a black eye. The better path is to make sure that when prospects look, they find a real person, in a format they can take in, with content that compliance approved and still under control. The four-year retention number has held steady for a long time. Leaders have told us that early activity matters. Our part is to give new producers something worth sharing, so a prospect's first impression is the producer and not just the company behind them. Prefer to listen? An audio version of this article is available https://publications.nxsmktg.com/whynewproducersstallbeforetheystart Readers who want to estimate the return on their marketing materials, and compare different ways of distributing them, can try Lynn’s interactive ROI calculator [ here ]; sharing contact information is optional. Lynn is also inviting one or two agencies to take part in a 90-day study of whether a personal, multi-format first impression speeds up early activity among new producers. Results will be shared anonymously. To learn more, contact her at lynn@lavender-landings.com Sources LIMRA, Building High-Performing Sales Teams , 2025 LIMRA Annual Conference: four-year retention of about 14%. LIMRA, Improving Financial Professional Retention Requires a Combination of Rewards and Reality , 2022: first-year retention of 44%–55%; causes of termination. LIMRA, Maximizing Sales Talent to Accelerate Growth , 2025, citing The Path to Improving Retention, LIMRA-Finseca, 2022: five factors in two-year retention. Capgemini Research Institute and LIMRA, World Life Insurance Report 2027 press release , Sept. 10, 2026. Dale Hall, Making Life Insurance Easier to Understand: Cracking the Code with Behavioral Science , Society of Actuaries, March 2026, summarizing the SOA Research Institute and RGA report Searching for Simplicity (2024). Field leaders also listed lack of early activity among the causes of termination. Four of those five factors are about the producer: who we hire and how we train and support them. Early activity is different. It depends on two people: the producer must reach out, and the prospect has to respond. Prospects respond to people they feel a connection with. What constitutes activity? When I began, it meant 10 meetings a week with new prospects, all of them in person. You left behind a business card and a generic company brochure and hoped you'd made enough of an impression to earn a second appointment. Today, a new producer may reach out in person or virtually. Either way, the takeaway must be memorable. A business card or marketing piece that provides an experience rather than just data can raise a producer's MQ (memorability quotient) significantly. The format gap Producers are largely on their own in building trust, and the materials they're handed don't help much. The World Life Insurance Report 2027, published in September 2026 by Capgemini and LIMRA, surveyed 6,175 consumers in 18 countries. More than 40% of those considering coverage felt confused, uncertain, or unconvinced by what they found, and one in four dropped out before buying. Overly technical language was the top reason, cited by 37%. Eighty-five percent of those consumers want to interact with an advisor at some point, and two-thirds prefer a human advisor when they finalize coverage. The demand for the producer is there. The materials can get in the way instead of advancing the relationship. Research shows what helps. In an experiment by the Society of Actuaries Research Institute and RGA, summaries, FAQs, and simple icons raised comprehension by 21%. Interactive elements, such as a needs calculator, raised it by 28%. On a page that used both, adding video raised it another 15%. Imagine delivering all that through something as simple as a business card. People, both prospects and producers, differ in many ways. Finding commonality is key to establishing a relationship. Half of consumers in the Capgemini–LIMRA study said they prefer advisors with similar demographic characteristics. And in the SOA–RGA experiment, comprehension rose significantly when participants saw the presenter as credible, expert, and from a similar cultural background. As a long-term care insurance wholesaler, I often funded advisors' client events: dinners meant to turn prospects into clients. Most guests didn't know the advisor or had only a passing acquaintance with him. At one event I sponsored, the advisor spent little time presenting himself and concentrated on the features and benefits of the coverage from the company I represented. He didn't convert a single prospect, and I got zero return on my investment. The guests had no reason to trust the person in front of them, so the product never had a chance. We can't know in advance who is on the other end of a producer's outreach. Some prospects read. Some watch. Some listen. Some need to try a calculator before they believe anything. The safest approach is to offer something for each of them, with the producer's own face and voice up front. Conventional e-newsletters contribute to inbox glut Most new producers are sent out with the same tools as everyone else: a business card, perhaps a company newsletter, and a set of pre-approved PDFs. The newsletter is the piece most firms count on to keep prospects warm, and it has five weaknesses. They are too long. Attention spans are short, and screen after screen asks for more time than most readers will give. They make readers scroll to choose. Readers scroll down to see what's there, then back up to decide. Many give up first. They are mostly text. Email can carry video and interactive tools, but few firms use them. Prospects who would rather watch or listen find little to engage them. They lack creative calls to action or lead magnets of value. Readers see a "Subscribe" or "Get my 5 tips" button as permission to receive spam. They speak for the company, not the person. Prospects learn about the carrier's strength and products, but nothing about the producer who sent it. There is also a compliance cost. Approved PDFs get downloaded, forwarded, and kept long after they've been revised. A PDF attached in March can still be circulating in October, carrying last spring's disclosure. Meanwhile, new producers who need to be noticed improvise with homemade posts and flyers. Producers need to be seen, and compliance needs control. A better newsletter respects the reader's time: one page with links to no more than three pieces of content. At a glance, the reader sees each title, whether it's an article, a video, or a podcast, and about how long it will take. They choose in seconds, without scrolling, in the format they prefer. And because the pieces are links, not downloads, compliance retains more control. What a first impression could be Social media posts, newsletters, mail, and product information all have their place in the sales cycle, but on their own, none of them builds a relationship. Today's technology can ease the tension between sales and compliance. Personal profiles with video and text, built on a company-approved template, let every producer present themselves authentically by email, on social media and websites, and through "phygital" marketing: digital content delivered through physical objects such as business cards, printed materials, or promotional merchandise. An agency or firm can start with business cards, where a scan or a tap opens a short personal video scripted to feature the "who" and not the "what" along with their bio, contact information, and compliance-approved content. Data alone isn't memorable. Experiences are. The company brochure can travel the same way. Printed brochures are costly and usually end up in the circular file. The same approved piece can live behind the producer's card instead, with no reprint charges, unlimited distribution, and home-office updates that take effect everywhere at once. Stories engage far better than statistics. Say a new producer targets young couples buying their first home who need to protect their mortgage. They need life insurance, and so do growing families and pre-retirees who want to transfer wealth efficiently. A firm could offer a choice of short, approved videos, each speaking to a different audience, that drop into the same approved brochure that explains different types of life insurance. Then add a lead gate, a short form that asks for a prospect's contact details in exchange for content of value. In large organizations, lead gates usually sit on the company website, not on individual producers' pages, so the contact information goes to the company or agency. Placed in the producer's own piece, a lead gate helps a new producer build a prospect list from the first week. Put together, these elements give a new producer something memorable that builds trust: a personal profile, an approved multimedia brochure, and a way to find the people worth calling. No study yet measures the effect directly, but the evidence points the same way. What leaders can do now None of this requires a new distribution model. It requires looking at a new producer's first 90 days from the prospect's side of the table. Audit the first impression. Gather everything a new producer can send a prospect in week one. Then ask: Why would I choose this producer over another? Put the person up front. Give each new producer a short video or audio introduction about who they are, not what they do. All your producers do similar work. Who they are is what sets them apart. Cover every format. Pair each key message with something to read, something to watch or hear, and something to try. In a newsletter, that means no more than three pieces, each labeled with its format and length. Host it; don't attach it. Sharing content by link keeps the company in control and ensures only approved, up-to-date materials circulate. Watch the early signals. Lack of activity is an early warning sign, and analytics can now measure it. Managers can see which channels drive activity and which new recruits may need help sooner. Have it ready before the first appointment. A fast start depends on what the producer can share in the first week, not the first quarter. Give them something worth answering Pushing prospects with a stick instead of offering a carrot gives the industry a black eye. The better path is to make sure that when prospects look, they find a real person, in a format they can take in, with content that compliance approved and still under control. The four-year retention number has held steady for a long time. Leaders have told us that early activity matters. Our part is to give new producers something worth sharing, so a prospect's first impression is the producer and not just the company behind them. Prefer to listen? An audio version of this article is available https://publications.nxsmktg.com/whynewproducersstallbeforetheystart Readers who want to estimate the return on their marketing materials, and compare different ways of distributing them, can try Lynn’s interactive ROI calculator [ here ]; sharing contact information is optional. Lynn is also inviting one or two agencies to take part in a 90-day study of whether a personal, multi-format first impression speeds up early activity among new producers. Results will be shared anonymously. To learn more, contact her at lynn@lavender-landings.com Sources LIMRA, Building High-Performing Sales Teams , 2025 LIMRA Annual Conference: four-year retention of about 14%. LIMRA, Improving Financial Professional Retention Requires a Combination of Rewards and Reality , 2022: first-year retention of 44%–55%; causes of termination. LIMRA, Maximizing Sales Talent to Accelerate Growth , 2025, citing The Path to Improving Retention, LIMRA-Finseca, 2022: five factors in two-year retention. Capgemini Research Institute and LIMRA, World Life Insurance Report 2027 press release , Sept. 10, 2026. Dale Hall, Making Life Insurance Easier to Understand: Cracking the Code with Behavioral Science , Society of Actuaries, March 2026, summarizing the SOA Research Institute and RGA report Searching for Simplicity (2024). items.extracted_text: Reinsurance renewals running later than usual, focus remains largely on price: Althoff, Hannover Re - Artemis.bm Reinsurance renewals running later than usual, focus remains largely on price: Althoff, Hannover Re 25th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Sven Althoff, Member of the Executive Board for Property & Casualty at Hannover Re, explained this morning that the reinsurance renewals are running later than usual in many areas and while rate adequacy is expected for many parts of the portfolio, he acknowledged there may be a need to start cycle managing due to price pressures. Speaking during the Hannover Re investor day held in London today, Althoff said that with the January 2027 renewals running behind their typical end of year schedule, it means data points are still lacking as to how much rates may move at 1/1. Althoff explained that as the January 2027 reinsurance renewals approach, pressure on the pricing environment continues to be seen, echoing what was discussed with Hannover Re’s clients at the Monte Carlo event in September. He said, “We have a later than usual renewal in many corners, so therefore I cannot speak about many data points yet. But the early data points we have would confirm that the focus is very much on price, particularly in the property cat space. “We have more discussions on terms and conditions with clients, but still very client specific rather than broad trends.” Echoing back to the Monte Carlo event again, Althoff continued to explain, “During the conference, we also talked more about structures with clients, translating into the direction of travel that there should be a little more demand in the market compared to the ’26 underwriting year. “However, at this stage, clients are mostly in the market with their expiring core structures.” Althoff highlighted the risk environment, which Hannover Re sees as complex, but this also drives greater client needs. “For us, that means there’s still strong demand for adequate pricing, and therefore we still expect that the rates will remain mostly adequate for the majority of our portfolio, which should, for 2027, create a situation where we will have selected growth opportunities,” Althoff said. Adding that, “But, at the same time, there will also be parts of our portfolio where we will have to start cycle managing due to the pricing pressure.” He continued to explain, “We have a heightened risk landscape, and the increase in the insured values both lead to a higher demand for reinsurance, and particularly reinsurance placed with reliable long-term partners that have a proven track record of providing capacity across the cycle and being shock absorbers in more challenging times by paying complex claims. “So, therefore, we feel we are well positioned across the cycle to further gain market share in an overall growing market as Hanover Re.” Althoff further stated, “The basis for this very much is our consistent and disciplined underwriting approach, and the very strong client relationships we have been able to build. In addition, we should also mention our use of retrocession, but also our approach to reserving to manage the earnings volatility and therefore the pricing cyclicality of the business. “Looking into the future in a more softer market environment, competitive advantages like our lower cost ratio or the higher share of the flexible costs via the broker distribution, will enable us to find profitable growth opportunities even in a more challenging rate environment, and it will keep the profitability of the business we write at attractive levels.” Hannover Re CEO Clemens Jungsthöfel also stated during his comments at the investor day, that in P&C reinsurance the reinsurer is prepared to utilise cycle management where necessary, to manage its portfolio and profitability in the soft market environment. Althoff later explained during the Q&A that, “On the portfolio composition in P&C, that should stay roughly the same. We see the most pressure when it comes to pricing on the property catastrophe side, but that has been a growing class for us. items.title: When Customers Get Their Own Chatbot Agent
items.original_title: When Customers Get Their Own Chatbot Agent
items.rss_title: When Customers Get Their Own Chatbot Agent
items.rss_description: When Customers Get Their Own Chatbot Agent PaulCarroll Sun, 11/22/2026 - 21:48 For some years now, I've been developing what I call the Laws of Zero. The notion is that the price of certain digital goods looks like it's headed toward zero if you map the cost curve out five or 10 years -- computing power, communication, sensors and cameras, in particular, have all seen exponential declines. So you should plan as though you will have an infinite supply of those goods. Thinking about zero cost has been a useful exercise for businesses... but AI is now driving the cost of intelligence toward zero, too, which will provide what feel like infinite amounts of it to customers. They're going to use it. We've already seen how AI has changed online search and started to alter many shopping behaviors. But AI agents will also mean that there will be essentially zero marginal cost for customers who want to request an update on an insurance claim, who want to complain, who want to challenge a bill, or who want any other sort of service. Meta's recent announcement of its Muse personal agent is just the start. The floodgates are about to open. Let's have a look. The positive response to Meta's announcement shows that the clock has started ticking on the trend toward vastly more customer service contacts. There will be the usual sorts of growing pains as the technology is being adopted -- there have already been reports of the AI agent getting into user data, such as bank records, that were supposed to be off limits -- so you won't be inundated right away. But the change is coming, so you might as well start planning. Think about all the calls you don't make and emails you don't send about a product or service you've bought because you don't have the time or just don't want to deal with the hassle. Lots of companies make considerable profit off the fact that people don't get around to canceling subscriptions. Then imagine what happens when someone can just tell an agent to make that contact -- or when the agent simply does the work on its own because it knows you want it to. That ease of contact issue hit home for me a couple of months ago, when my older daughter wrote an article for the Travel section of the Wall Street Journal. In my 17 years at the WSJ, the most letters I got on an article was maybe 300, and my daughter beat that on her first try. There were close to 300 comments on the article, and she received maybe 200 emails routed through the WSJ. The reason -- other than the fact that she wrote a great piece -- was that readers back in the 1990s had to type out a letter, surely in a formal style, use White-Out to fix any errors, find the right address in the paper's masthead, address the envelope, put a stamp on it and mail it. With my daughter, an online reader just had to hit the "comment" button or the "email" button and start typing. Ease of access will cause the same sort of increase in contacts for insurance companies. Meta even used a question about an insurance bill as an example of what Muse Wonder can do in an initial promotional video. (The example begins at the 2:27 mark here .) A couple of initial thoughts on how to get ready: For starters, you want to do everything you can to reduce the need for customers to wonder about anything. Amazon, in its early days, treated every contact by a customer as signifying a failure, and you should adopt that same mindset. I realize that will be far harder in insurance, with its complex processes and contracts, than it is in book selling. Still, every question that doesn't arise is one you don't have to figure out how to answer. Every update you provide is one the customer or their AI agent doesn't have to request. You'll also want to think about how to make your systems as accessible as possible to AI -- within privacy restrictions, regulation, etc. That effort will include sorting out which queries are from an AI, so you can have your AI deal with the customers' agents as much as possible and only bring in your human staff when necessary. The sooner you get started planning for the onslaught of customer inquiries, the better prepared you'll be. Zero is a magic number. Free is an unbeatable cost. Cheers, Paul P.S. If you're intrigued by my favorite topic, the Laws of Zero, the most complete explanation I've developed is in a book I wrote with Chunka Mui and Tim Andrews, " A Brief History of a Perfect Future: Inventing the World We Can Proudly Leave Our Kids by 2050 ." Image Paul Carroll While the focus to this point has been on customers potentially using AI agents to shop for insurance, people will also use them to demand much more service. Much more. There will be the usual sorts of growing pains as the technology is being adopted -- there have already been reports of the AI agent getting into user data, such as bank records, that were supposed to be off limits -- so you won't be inundated right away. But the change is coming, so you might as well start planning. Think about all the calls you don't make and emails you don't send about a product or service you've bought because you don't have the time or just don't want to deal with the hassle. Lots of companies make considerable profit off the fact that people don't get around to canceling subscriptions. Then imagine what happens when someone can just tell an agent to make that contact -- or when the agent simply does the work on its own because it knows you want it to. That ease of contact issue hit home for me a couple of months ago, when my older daughter wrote an article for the Travel section of the Wall Street Journal. In my 17 years at the WSJ, the most letters I got on an article was maybe 300, and my daughter beat that on her first try. There were close to 300 comments on the article, and she received maybe 200 emails routed through the WSJ. The reason -- other than the fact that she wrote a great piece -- was that readers back in the 1990s had to type out a letter, surely in a formal style, use White-Out to fix any errors, find the right address in the paper's masthead, address the envelope, put a stamp on it and mail it. With my daughter, an online reader just had to hit the "comment" button or the "email" button and start typing. Ease of access will cause the same sort of increase in contacts for insurance companies. Meta even used a question about an insurance bill as an example of what Muse Wonder can do in an initial promotional video. (The example begins at the 2:27 mark here .) A couple of initial thoughts on how to get ready: For starters, you want to do everything you can to reduce the need for customers to wonder about anything. Amazon, in its early days, treated every contact by a customer as signifying a failure, and you should adopt that same mindset. I realize that will be far harder in insurance, with its complex processes and contracts, than it is in book selling. Still, every question that doesn't arise is one you don't have to figure out how to answer. Every update you provide is one the customer or their AI agent doesn't have to request. You'll also want to think about how to make your systems as accessible as possible to AI -- within privacy restrictions, regulation, etc. That effort will include sorting out which queries are from an AI, so you can have your AI deal with the customers' agents as much as possible and only bring in your human staff when necessary. The sooner you get started planning for the onslaught of customer inquiries, the better prepared you'll be. Zero is a magic number. Free is an unbeatable cost. Cheers, Paul P.S. If you're intrigued by my favorite topic, the Laws of Zero, the most complete explanation I've developed is in a book I wrote with Chunka Mui and Tim Andrews, " A Brief History of a Perfect Future: Inventing the World We Can Proudly Leave Our Kids by 2050 ." Image Paul Carroll While the focus to this point has been on customers potentially using AI agents to shop for insurance, people will also use them to demand much more service. Much more. items.extracted_text: Hannover Re Capital Partners seeing "quite huge interest" from investors: Sehm - Artemis.bm Hannover Re Capital Partners seeing “quite huge interest” from investors: Sehm 25th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Speaking at Hannover Re’s investor day in London today, board member Silke Sehm explained that investor interest in ILS management unit Hannover Re Capital Partners is significant, while fellow-board member Sven Althoff explained why the reinsurer has so far not ventured into casualty ILS or other lines of business. Hannover Re Executive Board Member Silke Sehm noted that all insurance-linked securities activities continue to increase across the company’s different areas of focus, from facilitation and service provision, through to the more recent addition of ILS investment management under the Bermuda-based Hannover Re Capital Partners unit. Sehm explained, “On our fee income business, we are further increasing business in all of our ILS activities. So HCP, Hannover Re Capital Partners, but also on our other ILS activity, be it on the collateralized fronting side, also the cat bond transformer business, we are growing there. “But, especially with HCP, Hannover Re Capital Partners, quite huge interest from investors to connect our nat cat business with third-party capital, so we are on a good journey on that.” Sehm later explained that Hannover Re’s corporate strategy shows priorities are accessing risk, evaluating risk and transforming risk, with the ILS business highly relevant strategically. “We started 30 years ago with our K quota share, so first securitization. Then we built up our whole ILS unit 20 years ago, and the new venture is HCP Hannover Re Capital Partners, so where we bring also nat cat risk to the capital market, and we also have done this successfully on cyber activities. And I can imagine more of this in the future,” she explained. Sven Althoff, board member for the P&C business at Hannover Re, further commented in response to questions about how Hannover Re thinks about the evolution of third-party capital use in reinsurance. Althoff first noted that Hannover Re has not changed its approach to alternative capital and ILS, saying, “When it comes to the alternative capital question, this is a broader question today than it was a few years back. So what hasn’t changed at all, is that in the property space we have various ILS activities, be it collateralized fronting, be it transformer activities in the cat bond space, but also in the retrocessional area where we have worked together with ILS fund managers for a very long time. “That isn’t changing at all, particularly on the retrocessional side. That is, of course a significant part of our capital planning. So in that sense, that has not changed at all. But the product offering has become broader.” Althoff continued, “We now see casualty ILS emerging over the last two years. We see multi-class facilitation backed by alternative capital. In those two areas we are not playing today. “That is not a fundamental position. But if I, for example, look at casualty ILS, the transactions we have seen in the market would require us to take tail-end risk, whether it’s coming from the commutation side or whether it comes through the implied loss ratio caps that don’t mirror the original transaction, and we are not minded to take that risk. “If we see other structures, we may become a player in that space, but for now we don’t.” Later, Althoff commented more on alternative capital use with respect to facilities and follow-form arrangements and how Hannover Re views those trends. “We obviously observe that space. I mean, the facilitisation mostly happens in the typical wholesale markets, where you can bundle big pools of premium in order to make it attractive enough for third-party capital. Whether that trend is to stay or short-lived is of course difficult to answer,” Althoff said. Adding, “What we can say so far, is that the direct impact, whether it’s re-syndicates or the broker facilities you are talking about, to the allocation of capacity to Hanover Re has been very limited. So the capacity that was allocated to us was stable so far, and where we wanted to grow, we could grow. “But of course there is an indirect impact from the facilitisation. If you only have to place X percent of a slip versus 100 percent, it’s adding pressure on the pricing cycle, and there clearly we also feel the indirect impact of the facilitation. “But the proof of the pudding, of course, will be what is going to happen when the industry is not printing high-teens, low 20’s of ROE, and whether that capacity is to stay or not and we all don’t know the answer.” Also read: Reinsurance renewals running later than usual, focus remains largely on price: Althoff, Hannover Re . items.title: What Do AI Damage Estimates Bring to the Claims Table?
items.original_title: What Do AI Damage Estimates Bring to the Claims Table?
items.rss_title: What Do AI Damage Estimates Bring to the Claims Table?
items.rss_description: Bringing two sides on anything together seems less than likely in an increasingly polarized world. But some believe that artificial intelligence has a chance to bring two opposites closer to an unlikely agreement. AI-generated damage estimates could, through cold, hard …
items.extracted_text: What Do AI Damage Estimates Bring to the Claims Table? Article 0 Comments Bringing two sides on anything together seems less than likely in an increasingly polarized world. But some believe that artificial intelligence has a chance to bring two opposites closer to an unlikely agreement. AI-generated damage estimates could, through cold, hard data, bring policyholders and payers closer together on insurance claims payouts. Joe Ledbetter, a senior developer at Encircle, a claims app, believes the first steps toward a closer agreement between the two parties are already being taken. “There is AI usage on both ends, on both sides of the aisle, and they’re coming to a convergence within the claims process that is demonstrating a more accurate dollar value between the two parties,” Ledbetter said. “So, AI, on both sides, unintentionally, when they come together, they are actually more aligned than they were with just two humans assembling files trying to get aligned.” Related: APCIA Says Claims Data Standards in Works to Better Combat Criticism Ledbetter said his firm is putting out roughly 1,000 AI scopes a day by taking field data and running it through their AI, which produces the entire scope of work and then puts that into Xactimate. “So, what I can tell you is that the contractor’s data is 90% more accurate today and more complete today than it was without any of these tools,” Ledbetter said. “And so, the contractor side is seeing far more accurate estimates and scopes being produced on job files because AI is in the background making sure they don’t miss anything.” Simplifying the claims process with AI and technology has become a ubiquitous industry news refrain, but that doesn’t mean everyone is going to be happy with these developments. According to Mark Garrett, a director in the insurance intelligence and analytics practice at J.D. Power, technology may improve estimates and streamline processes, but claimants do not always have a better experience. J.D. Power surveys have found that, in some cases, customers feel that the photos they take and submit through a claims app go unused or unseen. “So, what I can tell you is from the customer process standpoint, it’s a big problem if they go through all the hassle submitting photos,” Garrett said. He said claimants are more likely to feel they went through unnecessary effort to get compensated for a loss when they are asked to take additional steps after submitting photos and claim details, such as taking their vehicle to a shop for a final estimate. Related: As AI Laws Proliferate, Liability and Coverage Questions Multiply “What that can do, though, is create huge slowdowns in the process,” Garrett said. “If they tear down the car, the shop’s starting to work on things and they realize ‘Oh yeah all this was missed in that AI estimate,’ that alone can add days. We’re not talking about an hour or same-day approval. We’re talking about five or six days for a carrier to get back to the shop, then maybe they ask questions and the shop’s got to respond back.” Nuha Hashem, co-founder and chief technology officer of Cozmo AI, believes that all the steps involved in the traditional claims process are one reason the two parties’ estimates often come in so far apart. She describes that process as someone reporting damage to an adjuster by phone or digitally, followed by a manual sketch of the damage and then a digital version of that sketch. Photos must be uploaded with notes, which are handed to a desk estimator for review. That all goes into Xactimate, where line items and codes are entered. “The work that these people are doing right now, they don’t have to go through all of this manual work,” Hashem said. “They just have to focus on talking with the customer, making sure the work is done to the standards.” Timothy Wieneke, president and managing director of Wieneke Group, which provides property claims services, decided to try an experiment that led to him creating an AI-based tool that generated estimates in about 30 seconds. “Its accuracy was about 90-95% on roofs,” he wrote in response to a reporter’s LinkedIn post asking for insight and comments from claims professionals about their experience with AI damage estimates. That wasn’t his only experiment with AI and damage estimates, a tale he shared as a point of caution. “The bigger thing was what I learned in the process of making it. I can tell you, in depth, how to manipulate AI to create estimates to look like whatever you want,” said Wieneke, who conducted the AI experiment as part of a conference presentation on AI. “I showed specific prompts that instruct AI to manipulate estimate results. I can make AI manipulate the same scope of work down by 50% or triple it with the right prompting.” The lesson he came away with is that the industry needs to “get out ahead of AI.” “I’m starting to see it being used to create estimates that look legitimate but raise serious questions,” he added. Ledbetter said AI damage estimates are not only bringing valuations closer but also helping to improve documentation. He’s already seeing contractors improving on this. “They’re putting really good claim package together with estimates and PDF reports and drying logs and photos,” he said. On the other side, he is seeing carriers working to create efficiencies, building streamlined intake processes. “Then they have an LLM, an AI tool, read all of that context and digest it and then what those tools are traditionally looking for are the gaps or the holes or the missing information,” he said. Ledbetter said a carrier may flag an estimate that bills for three days of drying when the claim file contains documentation for only the first two days. The missing documentation for the third day does not necessarily mean the work was not performed, but it creates a gap for the carrier to review. Alok Kumar, co-founder of Cozmo AI, believes it’s not just the data that will better align claimants and insurers. He believes the push and pull between the two will balance out with a structured data set aligned with industry standards, laws, regulations and contracts. “So, I believe once you have common datasets, then it’s a black and white,” Kumar said. “Today, it’s not a black and white. That’s because a 10-year-experience human estimator has a different point of view than a one-year-experience human estimator. So, when you can actually bridge that gap with pure data and numbers, then it ceases to be gray or spectrums of gray.” Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.title: Technology outages underscore need to review cyber coverage
items.original_title: Technology outages underscore need to review cyber coverage
items.rss_title: Technology outages underscore need to review cyber coverage
items.rss_description: Businesses seeking insurance protection against technology outages should ensure their cyber policies cover both nonmalicious system failures and business interruptions caused by disruptions at outside technology providers, insurance experts say.
items.extracted_text: Policies vary widely, and coverage for failures at third-party providers may require extensions that carry additional premiums, sublimits or longer waiting periods, they said. Earlier this month, a series of technology outages disrupted Microsoft’s email and other services worldwide, forced the Federal Aviation Administration to temporarily halt departures nationwide, delayed United Airlines flights and affected JPMorgan Chase’s banking operations and several Apple services. Government officials and affected companies said there was no evidence that the outages resulted from cyberattacks. Despite the widespread disruption caused by the Microsoft outage, insured losses are expected to be relatively limited , with waiting periods, retentions and the difficulty of demonstrating financial losses potentially limiting recoveries. To cover such outages, cyber policies must include coverage for nonmalicious system failures under their dependent or contingent business interruption provisions, said Alan Lyons, New York-based partner and co-chair of the insurance, reinsurance and dispute resolution group at Herrick Feinstein. “Coverage for non-malicious system failures and for failures at third-party providers is more often an extension, may carry a sublimit, and may come with a longer waiting period, all of which can mean additional premium. How much it costs, and whether it’s offered at all, varies by insurer,” he said. The recent Microsoft technology outage is an example of the “standard dependent business interruption type of risk exposure, where you’re reliant upon a technology service provider for revenue generation for your business,” said Meredith Schnur, New York-based U.S. and Canada cyber practice leader at Marsh Risk. Many cyber policies include dependent business interruption coverage for disruptions at technology providers, but whether an individual policy responds depends on its terms and the circumstances of the loss, she said. Broader coverage does not necessarily cost more, Ms. Schnur said, noting that direct premium comparisons are difficult because policies differ significantly. Many U.S. policyholders buy cyber coverage through endorsements to other policies, such as business owners policies, said Lou Botticelli, New York-based managing director and U.S. cyber brokerage leader at Howden. Packaged coverage may be less comprehensive than stand-alone cyber policies and could leave policyholders uninsured for certain technology failures, he said. Howden recommends stand-alone cyber policies with dedicated limits to provide broader protection, Mr. Botticelli said. Broader coverage may justify the additional cost, said Joshua Gold, a shareholder at Anderson Kill in New York office and co-chair of the cyber insurance recovery group. “It can cost more, but not nearly as much, in my view, as the benefits it yields,” he said. items.extracted_text: Twelve Securis hires Tse as Head of Singapore and Greater China - Artemis.bm Twelve Securis hires Tse as Head of Singapore and Greater China 25th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Twelve Securis, the specialist catastrophe bond and insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager, is continuing its expansion into Asian markets and has hired Bonny Tse as its first Head of Singapore and Greater China. Twelve Securis has been increasing its focus on the Asia Pacific region in recent years, seeing it as an area that offers many opportunities for the insurance-linked securities market to further expand and grow. Bonny Tse, an investment professional based in Singapore has joined Twelve Securis as its first Head of Singapore and Greater China, engaged under an Employer of Record (EOR) arrangement. The investment manager does not currently have a local office in Singapore, but is planning to launch a base in the region, potentially next year. Over her career, Tse has more than 15 years of specific experience in the asset management industry, with a specialism in institutional and intermediary business development across Asia. Her work has focused on initiating and securing mandates from institutional investors across the region, developing relationships with institutions and allocators, as well as driving new distribution initiatives. Most recently, Tse spent one year working as a Director of Funds Advisory at EFG Private Banking, prior to which she worked for more than twelve years at EFG Asset Management, culminating in a role as Director of Sales and Distribution, Asia. Earlier in her career, Tse worked at Nomura Asset Management in Hong Kong with a focus on business development in China and held roles at JP Morgan Asset Management and Janus Capital Group also in Hong Kong, while starting her career in 2001 at HSBC in Vancouver, Canada. As Twelve Securis builds out its ILS capabilities and distribution reach in Asia, Tse brings a wealth of experience and connections in key markets there. You can read more about Twelve Securis’ focus on the Asian market in our interview from earlier this year with Vittorio Sangiorgio, Head of Investment Solutions .
